source.title: Exploring Polyglot Harmony: On Multilingual Data Allocation for Large Language Models Pretraining
source.authors: Ping Guo; Yubing Ren; Bin-Bin Li; Feng-Ze Liu; Hao-Bin Lin; Yi-Fan Zhang; Bing-Ni Zhang; Tai-Feng Wang; Yin Zheng

record.file_problem: Whole paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests predictive scaling-law performance in multilingual pretraining with a new cross-lingual interaction-aware formulation, including extrapolation to a larger token budget.
record.gate_note: Table 1 reports fitting and extrapolation metrics for the proposed method and two scaling-law baselines. The paper also reports downstream benchmark comparisons for language-allocation methods, but those do not test whether downstream performance is predictable from scale or pretraining loss. The multilingual interaction-ratio plots and allocation results concern language proportions, not the parameter/token or parameter/compute split in the claim.
record.test_reason: The study evaluates held-out pretraining-loss predictions at 1T tokens using a multilingual scaling formulation fitted at smaller budgets. This bears on V2, although the reported 100B-to-1T comparison spans only one order of magnitude. Its fitting metrics do not independently establish V1's power-law dependence over several orders of magnitude.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors conclude that CLIMB better predicts multilingual validation losses and that its allocations improve benchmark performance at 1.2B and 7B parameters. Fitting and allocation estimation are primarily validated at 1.2B; explicitly incorporating model size and modeling transfer involving languages absent from training remain future work.
record.recipe_differences: Adapts monolingual data-scaling-law ideas into a multilingual interaction-aware effective-token formulation; it does not reproduce the original parameter/data/compute sweeps or compute-optimal parameter-token allocation method.
record.method_sensitivity: Predictive accuracy varies with token budget: it is limited below 25B tokens and improves above 25B. The paper also reports cross-lingual interaction-ratio behavior varying with language proportion, co-training languages, language count, and data scale, but these are not direct tests of the listed claim versions.

fits_no_version.finding: At 100B tokens, CLIMB fits multilingual validation losses better than Isolated and MSL, with R² of 0.978–0.992.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Accounting for cross-lingual interactions improves validation-loss prediction across language mixtures.

fits_no_version.finding: The proposed predictor is less accurate below 25B tokens and improves above that budget as transfer relationships stabilize.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Reliability of this multilingual interaction model depends on the training-data regime.

record.problems: The scaling-law evaluation uses 1.2B-parameter models and does not vary model size or compute. Prediction accuracy is explicitly limited below 25B tokens. Table 1 reports point metrics without uncertainty estimates.
record.rows_left_out: None of the reported Table 1 fitting or extrapolation values were left out. Downstream benchmark results and language-allocation outcomes were not extracted as rows because they do not measure the versions' predictive claims.

untested.parts: Power-law loss scaling in actual parameters, tokens or compute over several orders of magnitude with other bottlenecks controlled. Equation 3 assumes a monolingual power law; the main empirical evaluation concerns an interaction-adjusted multilingual predictor.

Extrapolation over multiple orders of magnitude, across model sizes or compute budgets, and applicability of unmodified power laws without effective-token corrections. The reported token-budget extrapolation is tenfold.
Compute-optimal parameter/token allocation and its scaling exponents; language-mixture optimization does not measure this split.
Architecture variation at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities or training regimes beyond text pretraining.
Quantitative prediction of downstream performance from scale or pretraining loss; benchmark comparisons evaluate allocation methods.
Dependence of fitted exponents or compute-optimal splits on setup or fitting choices, and direct tests of departures from a single power law.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text identifies this version as a preprint under review, so the record's NeurIPS peer-review attribution is unsupported. Table 1 supplies point metrics without uncertainty; it does not clearly specify the exact two fitting budgets or held-out mixture protocol. Low-data prediction limitations alone do not demonstrate failure of power-law scaling or small-to-large extrapolation.

versions.untested_parts: Tests multilingual validation-loss prediction using a token-budget and effective-language-allocation formulation. Does not test loss scaling with parameter count or training compute, or isolate regimes where the other scaling variables are not bottlenecks.
Tests extrapolation from fitting results at 100B training tokens to 1T tokens in multilingual settings; does not report extrapolation across parameter-count or compute scales.
The paper optimizes language proportions at a specified token budget; it does not test how loss-minimizing parameter count and token count scale with a fixed compute budget.
Does not vary depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
Studies multilingual text pretraining, not other modalities, repeated-data regimes, fine-tuning, or transfer regimes.
Reports downstream benchmark scores for different language allocations, but does not test whether downstream performance is predictably related to scale or pretraining loss.
Does not compare fitted exponents or compute-optimal parameter/token splits across fitting choices or setups, or test whether those curves depart from a single power law.

rows.subject: Transformer-based multilingual models (tested across 2-, 3-, 5-, and 16-language settings)
rows.operation_detail: Assess predictive accuracy of the cross-lingual interaction-aware scaling law across token budgets
rows.value: Limited below 25B tokens; markedly improves above 25B tokens as cross-lingual interactions become stable and predictable
rows.note: Authors state that predictive accuracy is limited in low-data regimes and improves at larger budgets.
rows.check: Section 3.3 describes low-budget prediction accuracy, without identifying an out-of-range extrapolation test or demonstrating failure of a simple power law. It cannot establish the claimed V1/V2 scope restriction.

relationships.condition: Interaction-adjusted CLIMB predictions at 1T tokens for fixed 1.2B-parameter models with 2, 3, 5 or 16 languages
relationships.reason: R29–R30, R35–R36, R41–R42 and R47–R48 report extrapolation R² of 0.936–0.964 and corrected Huber errors of 0.208–0.525 ×10−3; support is confined to the reported tenfold token extrapolation.
relationships.display_finding: Extrapolation R² ranged from 0.936 to 0.964, with corrected Huber errors of 0.208–0.525 ×10−3 at 1T tokens.

source_check.reason: R29–R30, R35–R36, R41–R42 and R47–R48 show accurate extrapolation: R² 0.936–0.964 and corrected Huber losses 0.208–0.525 ×10−3. Support covers the tested tenfold token extrapolation.

relationships.condition: Isolated and MSL baseline extrapolations at 1T tokens across all four language-count settings

relationships.display_finding: Across all four language settings at 1T tokens, R² was 0.648–0.767 for Isolated and 0.830–0.852 for MSL.
